If a customer reverts to their birth name from their married or civil partnership name but they had a change of name in between (for example, when a customer changed their birth name by deed poll and then again by marriage or civil partnership), you must:
ask the customer for:
their full birth certificate (you may accept the short birth certificate as long as it shows you all of the information you need)
the official documents showing the change of name from their birth name to their most recent name in use. This could include change of name deeds, their marriage or divorce document, civil partnership or final order that shows their birth name and the previous married or civil partner name
a signed statement to explain they are reverting to their birth name
evidence they use the birth name for all official purposes
use the customer’s passport history records to make sure you can see the link between all of the name changes from the birth name to the married or civil partner name
If you cannot see the link between all the name changes (for example, the passport history is not clear or there is no record on the passport history of a change of name document) you must:
ask the customer for the change of name documents that shows the link from the birth name to the married or civil partner name
ask for evidence that shows the customer was using the names (if the customer cannot provide the change of name document)
consider if you have enough information that shows the link from the birth name to the married or civil partner name
If you are not satisfied with the link from the birth name to the married or civil partner name, you must treat the change as a new change of name and ask for evidence:
of a change of name (or example, statutory declaration)
they use the name for all purposes
Customer reverts to a name that is not their birth name
Some customers may:
revert to a previous name that is not their birth name, for example, to a:
previous married or civil partner name
a name they previously changed to by deed poll
change their name to a brand new name
If they do, you must treat it as a change of name and ask the customer for evidence:
of the change
they use the name for all purposes
Change of name: adult changed gender
If the customer has changed their name because they have changed gender, you must refer to name changes because the customer has changed gender.
Change of name: before, during, or after registration or naturalisation
If a customer changed their name before or during the naturalisation or registration process, they must tell UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI).
This is because the new name must be on the nationality certificate (see Change of name before or during naturalisation or registration).
You must refer to name changes and name differences after the customer has naturalised or registered, when dealing with:
changes of name after the customer naturalised or registered
differences with the customer’s name, after they registered or naturalised
Minor changes to forenames and surnames
We consider a minor change to a:
forename as:
a change to the spelling (for example, from Lesley to Leslie)
a change to the order of the forenames
adding or dropping a hyphen between 2 forenames (as long as a forename does not become a surname or a surname does not become a forename)
dropping one or more forenames unless it is their first forename
surname as:
the adding or removing of a hyphen on a double barrelled name
We do not consider adding a forename as a minor change of name. If a customer does, they must provide evidence that they have changed their name and use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
If a customer uses their previous surname as a new forename, as they have married or entered in to a civil partnership, you must refer to non-dual citizens who use their previous surname as an additional forename.
As long as the customer provides 2 pieces of evidence showing they use the name for all official purposes, we will accept applications that show a minor change to the:
forename(s) for first time adult applications; or,
forename(s) or surname(s) on a renewal or replacement application
Minor forename changes: first time adult applications
The customer may tell you the name on their application has changed slightly from the name on their supporting documents.
You must:
Tell the customer you will issue a passport using the name on the:
application, if they provide 2 pieces of evidence to show they use the name for all official purposes
birth certificate with an observation to show they are also known as [name on application form], if they do not provide 2 pieces of evidence to show they use the name for all official purposes
Make sure the name correctly shows on the system, by using the name on the:
birth certificate (if the customer does not provide 2 pieces of evidence to show they use the name for all official purposes)
application (if the customer provides 2 pieces of evidence to show they use the name for all official purposes)
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you’ve made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Issue the passport.
Adding or removing a hyphen on a double-barrelled surname
If a customer adds or removes a hyphen on a double barrelled surname without any evidence, we will accept the name, as long as:
they have not changed the spelling or order of their name; and,
they are applying for a first time passport application
You must deal with the application in line Minor changes on renewal and replacement applications, when the customer is:
removing the hyphen on a double-barrelled surname; and,
renewing or replacing their passport
Minor changes on renewal and replacement applications
When a customer sends a renewal or replacement application with a minor change to their name (for example, Michael to Micheal), you must:
tell the customer you will issue a passport in the name on their old passport, unless they give you 2 pieces of evidence that shows they use the name for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
If a customer tells you they will send the evidence, you must:
Use the Comms builder to send the ‘Change in personal details for adults’ email template to the customer. This template asks the customer to send HM Passport Office evidence they use their name on the passport application.
Deal with the change of name, in line with current guidance when you get the evidence.
The customer may tell you to use the name shown on the old passport.
You must:
Update the name on the system with the name on their old passport.
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Middle name held old passport: not on new application
The customer’s old passport may show a middle name, but the customer does not include it on their renewal or replacement application and there is no evidence to show they have changed their name.
You must:
Update the name on the system to include the customer’s middle name, as shown on their old passport.
Deal with the application (in line with current guidance).
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Middle name on new application: not on the old passport
If the old passport does not show a middle name but the renewal or replacement application shows one, you must consider why. For example, it may not have originally been included because:
of an error (for example, the customer never changed their name and it should have been on the previous passport)
the customer changed their name by statutory declaration (to remove the middle name)
If the middle name was not originally included because:
the customer formally changed their name (to remove it) and they now want to include it, they must provide us with evidence of a change of name and evidence they use it for all official purposes
we previously treated it as a minor change of name, they must provide us with 2 pieces of evidence they use the name (so we can treat it as a minor change to add it back on)
of an error (meaning it should have originally been included) we can accept the customer’s birth certificate that shows the middle name, as evidence
You must:
Tell the customer what evidence to send (depending on why the middle name was not originally included).
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Previous passport names in a different order to the application
If the order of the forename and middle names on the old passport is different to the order of the names on the renewal or replacement application, you must contact the customer and ask them to confirm the name they use for all official purposes.
The customer may want their forename and middle name on their passport in the same order as on their old passport.
You must:
Update the names on the system so that they match the name on the old passport.
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
If the customer wants their name in the new order they’ve put on their application form, ask them to send you 2 pieces of evidence that shows they use it for all official purposes (see evidence to change a name).
Name on old passport: different spelling to application
When the spelling of a forename or middle name on the customer’s old passport is different to the spelling on their renewal or replacement application, you must contact them and ask them to confirm the name they use for all official purposes.
The customer may want the passport in the same spelling as their old passport.
You must:
Update the name the system so it matches the name on the old passport.
Add a case note show all actions taken and decisions made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
If the customer wants the name in the new spelling, you must ask them to send 2 pieces of evidence that shows they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Name on old passport: in a different order to the application
When a customer’s forename and surname on their old passport is in a different order to their name on the new passport, you must contact them and ask them to confirm the name they use for all official purposes.
The customer may want their passport issued in the name that is in the same order as on the old passport.
You must:
Update the name on the system so that it matches the name on the old passport.
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
If the customer wants their name in a new order, you must ask them to send evidence of the change of name and evidence they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Customer adding or removing a hyphen between 2 forenames
When a customer sends a renewal or replacement application and they add or remove a hyphen between 2 forenames, you must tell the customer you will issue a passport in the name on their old passport.
You can issue a passport using their new name if they give you 2 pieces of evidence that shows they use the name for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
If a customer tells you they will send you evidence, you must:
Put the application on hold, while you wait for their evidence.
Deal with the change of name, in line with current guidance when you get the evidence.
The customer may tell you to use the name shown on the old passport.
You must:
Update the name on the system with the name on their old passport.
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
When a name is considered unusual
If you accept a name change but you consider it to be unusual, you must first discuss the application with your line manager. If they agree, you must:
Tell the customer they must confirm in writing that they understand we cannot take responsibility for any difficulties they may have when they use their passport.
Keep a permanent record of the letter (see Document scans: scanning, uploading and redacting customer documents).
Changing a child’s name
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff how to deal with child applications that include a change of name.
When dealing with an application to change a child’s name you must use the guidance in this section with:
Authorisation and consent: needed to issue a passport and Who must consent to a child’s passport application to understand HM Passport Office’s definition of a child and when additional consent to a change of name is needed for children and young adults aged 16 and 17 years
change of name on British overseas citizen (BOCs) and British overseas territory citizen (BOTCs) applications, if the change of name is for a BOC or BOTC customer
name and change of name on diplomatic or official passport applications, if the application is for a diplomat or official
Digital Application Processing: change of name applications
Why a child’s name may be changed
A child’s name may be changed through:
a change of gender
an enrolled deed poll, unenrolled deed poll or change of name deed
adoption
the re-registration of their birth
an update to section 17 of an English or Welsh full birth certificate
a court order (including specific issues orders and overseas court orders)
a statutory declaration or affidavit
an act of Parliament
The new name the child uses must be acceptable for use in the passport. You, the examiner, must refer to:
names that cannot be used in the passport, for names:
that may cause public offence
the system cannot accept because of technical reasons
how to show uncommon names for:
names that have cultural or naming conventions (traditions that mean a name must be shown in a certain way)
Welsh names
Irish and Gaelic names
names that have junior prefixes or suffixes
stage, professional and religious names
customers who only have a single name
names that have titles
Any type of change to a child’s name is seen as a change of name, including:
dropping the forename or middle name
changing the spelling of the forename or surname
adding a forename, middle name or surname
changing the forename or middle name
changing the order of the forename and middle name
changing the surname
changing the full name
adding or removing a hyphen
Middle name is not included on an application
Customers may send us a renewal or replacement application for their child, without including their middle name, even though it was on their old passport. When this happens, we will issue a new passport in the same name as their old passport, unless we have:
evidence the child has changed their name and that they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
the consent of everyone with parental responsibility to change the name
You must add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Reducing the risk of fraud when a child’s name has changed
Most customers will change their name for genuine reasons. To reduce the risk of customers changing their name for fraudulent reasons, you must refer to the:
confirming identity guidance for any extra checks you must carry our when the customer has changed their name
risk indicators guidance, to check if the change of name is an indication of fraud
When changing a child’s name, you must carry out checks on Passport records to make sure there is not an existing or expired passport held in a previous version of the name.
Case noting and scanning when a child’s name is changed
When using this guidance to change a child’s name, you, the examiner, must refer to Names: name related case notes to make sure the case notes include all the correct information.
All documents received in support of a child’s application must be added to the application by the Document Handling Unit (DHU). This includes applications received at a public counter.
Evidence we need to change a child’s name
When a child’s name has been changed, HM Passport Office need consent from everyone who holds parental responsibility for the child, and evidence:
of the change of name; and,
the new name is being used for all official purposes, except when the name has changed through:
adoption; or,
re-registration of a birth (this does not include updates to section 17 of an English or Welsh birth certificate, where evidence the name is being used for all official purposes is required in addition to the updated birth certificate)
You must refer to Names: evidence to change a name for what you can accept.
Change of name through adoption
When dealing with adoptions, you must refer to:
parent and guardian guidance
adoptions guidance
Names: aligning names on foreign documents, if an adopted child has a foreign passport in a different name
If a child’s name has changed through adoption, we do not need evidence they use the name for all official purposes or the consent of everyone who has parental responsibility, provided we have the full adoption certificate or adoption order.
If a customer sends a renewal or replacement application with an adoption certificate or order, you must:
make sure it includes a referee who has confirmed (or certified) a photo in the new name
manually cancel the old passport on our passport records (if the old name was not in section 2 of the application)
Changing a child’s name following birth re-registration
It is possible for a child’s name to change when the parents re-register the birth (see birth certificates guidance). When this happens, you do not need any other evidence of a change of name.
This does not include name changes because of names added to section 17 of a birth certificate issued in England or Wales, see Birth registration, English and Welsh birth certificates: section 17. Adding a name to this section of a birth certificate does not follow the same process as re-registration. For change of name purposes, when a name is added to section 17 of an English or Welsh birth certificate and the customer adopts this name, we need consent to the change of name from everyone who holds parental responsibility for the child.
Incorrect name on birth certificates
We must not tell the customer to take steps to correct the birth certificate to support their passport application.
If they tell us the name on their or their child’s birth certificate is wrong (before we use the correct name on the passport) they must provide us with evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
If the customer asks you how to correct the birth certificate, you must tell them they may only be able to change it, if they can show a mistake was made when they registered the birth and have evidence that the child was, either:
using a different name to the one on the birth certificate (at the time the child’s birth was registered)
has been known by a different name to the one on the birth certificate (from when they were born or shortly afterwards)
Any corrections to a birth certificate issued in England or Wales will be made using a ‘marginal note’ (a note added to the relevant section of the birth certificate). We can then issue the passport using the name in the marginal note.
Changing a child’s name because they have changed gender
If a child has changed their name because they have changed gender, you must refer to name changes because the customer has changed gender.
Changing a child’s name after they registered as British
You must refer to name changes and name differences after naturalisation or registration, when dealing with:
changes of name after the child registered as a British national
differences with the child’s name after they registered as a British national
Change of name after the passport was lost or stolen
Children who have changed their name after their passport was lost or stolen, must still provide evidence to show they have changed their name, in line with this guidance.
They must also report their passport lost or stolen when applying for a replacement passport.
Child’s name on collective passports
We need the signed and written consent of everyone with parental responsibility for a child to be included on a collective passport, if it’s in a different name to that on their:
full British passport (if they have one)
birth certificate or nationality certificate (if they do not have British passport)
Child change of name: consent to the change
Everyone with parental responsibility must give consent to change the name for anyone under the age of 16 (18 if the child has a care order or court order in place). Normally, both parents have parental responsibility, but others may get it through court orders or something similar. You must refer to parents and guardians: consent, when dealing with an international application that includes a court order relating to a child.
When dealing with a change of name for a child, you must:
consider who has parental responsibility
check that everyone with parental responsibility has given consent to change the child’s name
consider if there are any court orders that:
prevent the child’s name from being changed
allow the child’s name to be changed without the consent of everyone who has parental responsibility (see Parental responsibility: parents and guardians consent for types of court orders)
If it is unclear if the parent has sole parental responsibility, you must:
send letter 319 to the customer to ask them to confirm in writing, that they have sole responsibility
add a case note to show all of the actions and decisions you made
If someone with parental responsibility has died, you must refer to Parental responsibility: loco parentis or a person has died.
The legal basis for consent
We are guided by the legal position on who can change a child’s name. It is defined by case law and the judgement given by the Court of Appeal on case Re P (1997) 2 FLR 730.
The case was about whether a county council was obliged to recognise a change of surname for 3 children, when:
they were presented with a signed deed poll, as evidence of the change of name
the father (who had parental responsibility) did not give consent to change their names
The court’s decision was that the change of a child’s surname was fundamental and where there is a dispute and both parents have parental responsibility, either:
the consent of both parents is needed
a court order is needed that allows the change of name without the consent of everyone who has parental responsibility
To make sure we are consistent with the conditions of different parts of the UK, our approach to consent and parental responsibility applies to all child changes of name.
Child change of name: unable to get consent
We will not accept a child’s change of name unless everyone with parental responsibility has given their consent or there is a court order allowing the change of name. This includes when they are using their new name for all official purposes (for example, the new name is used with the NHS and child benefit but not everyone with parental responsibility has given consent for the child’s change of name).
Some customers may have difficulty getting the consent of someone else with parental responsibility. For example, because they no longer have contact with them, or there are safeguarding concerns.
If we cannot get the consent from everyone with parental responsibility, you must:
Follow Child change of name: vulnerable customers and children, if there are safeguarding concerns.
Call the customer to tell them they have the option of getting a court order, (for example, a specific issue order) allowing them to change the child’s name without the consent of everyone with parental responsibility (we must not insist they do it, as it is up to them to decide).
If a customer does not get a court order, you must:
Deal with the application, in line with current guidance.
Issue the passport in the child’s original name.
Tell the customer we cannot accept responsibility for any difficulties they may have (for example, because the child is using their new name for all other purposes).
Child change of name: vulnerable customers and children
We usually need the consent of everyone with parental responsibility to change a child’s name. Some customers may not be able to get the consent of someone with parental responsibility, if it would put their (or their child’s) welfare at risk (for example, if they may be subject to abuse). When this happens, you must refer to safeguarding: consent issues.
If you have any doubts about the consent being genuine, you must refer to the Authorisation and consent guidance.
Caveats (objections to a child having a passport)
A parent, or other interested party, can submit a caveat to a child having a passport.
If someone submits a caveat, you must refer to Authorisation and consent: needed to issue a passport when dealing with a passport application for a child. You must scan any documents about caveats on the system.
Change of parental responsibility during a name change
Someone else may get parental responsibility after everyone with parental responsibility already gave their consent to change a child’s name and got a change of name document (for example, statutory declaration).
We will accept the change of name without the new person’s consent, as long as everyone who had parental responsibility, consented to the change of name at the time.
When someone believes they have parental responsibility
If someone does not give consent to change a child’s name and they believe they have parental responsibility, you must give them 1 month to provide evidence to show it. If they:
provide you with evidence to show they have parental responsibility, you must only accept the change of name if they (and everyone else who has parental responsibility) gives their consent
do not provide us with evidence to show they have parental responsibility, you must accept the change of name (as long as everyone else who has parental responsibility gives their consent)
Child change of name: evidence of consent
In some cases, we may be able to check who has parental responsibility using the full birth certificate (see full birth certificate guidance).
A father will not automatically lose parental responsibility if they have been taken off a birth certificate. They will only lose parental responsibility if it is removed by a court order.
If there is evidence to suggest that someone else has parental responsibility, we will need their consent before we change a child’s name.
Statutory declarations: showing parental consent
Some customers may tell us in their statutory declaration that everyone with parental responsibility consented to the child’s change of name or is aware of it.
We will only accept the statutory declaration as evidence everyone with parental responsibility has given their consent, if it includes:
the names of everyone with parental responsibility
the signatures of everyone with parental responsibility
You must request additional consent to the change of name if you need it and confirm the consent is genuine when you receive it, before completing the child’s application.
Change of name deeds that show consent
Some change of name deeds may be signed by both parents. We will accept it, if there is no other evidence showing someone else also has parental responsibility.
You must request additional consent to the change of name if you need it and confirm the consent is genuine when you receive it, before completing the child’s application.
Enrolled deed poll that shows consent
When a customer sends us an enrolled deed poll, issued by the Supreme Court or High Court, as evidence of a change of name, we will not need the consent of everyone with parental responsibility. This is because the Enrolment of Deeds Regulations 1994 requires, either the:
consent of everyone with parental responsibility
reasons why the consent of everyone with parental responsibility could not be given
The Judge will take into account the lack of consent from anyone who has parental responsibility, before deciding to allow the change of name.
Child change of name consent: loco parentis or a person has died
If someone with parental responsibility has died, the customer must send us:
evidence of the change of name and evidence the child uses it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
any court orders that are in place (or confirmation there are none)
a written statement to explain the situation
the child’s birth certificate
the personal details of the person who has died and had parental responsibility (full name, date of birth and place and country of birth) and their passport number, if available (to see if we can find a record of them on passport records)
if their passport number is not available, the death certificate
When you, the examiner, receive the person’s, who is deceased, personal details and passport number (if this is available), you must check to see if:
The information provided matches the information on previous passport records, for example, the child’s previous applications, and the supporting documents provided, for example, the full birth certificate.
There is a passport number for the person, who is deceased, on the child’s previous applications, if no passport number has been provided.
Passport records confirm the passport is cancelled because the holder is deceased.
If our passport and application records do not show the holder is deceased or we cannot find a record of the person, you must request the death certificate of the person with parental responsibility.
If loco parentis applies, the customer must send us:
evidence of the change of name and evidence the child uses it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
evidence the customer is acting as loco parentis (see parents and guardians: consent guidance)
a court order that allows the customer to change the child’s name without the consent of everybody with parental responsibility
We must safeguard (protect) adults and children who may be at risk. If someone acting as loco parentis cannot provide evidence, you must raise a guidance query with the Quality and Examination Support team (QuESt).
Changing a child’s name when there is a court order
Court orders usually give leave (permission) to change a child’s name, instead of a document that formally changes their name. Because of this, we also need evidence a child has changed their name and evidence it’s being used for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
You must be careful when a passport application includes a:
change of name for a child
court order giving leave (or permission) to change the child’s name and 1 or more years have passed between the date it was issued and the date the customer sent the passport application
This is because, we:
cannot be certain the court order giving leave (or permission) to change the child’s name has been used
need to be sure the child uses the name for all official purposes
When this happens, you must:
Make sure you have evidence the child has changed their name and it’s being used for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Scan the evidence on to the application.
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Court orders that specifically include a change of name
Some court orders may specifically say that a child is now known by a new name. When this happens, you must:
Not ask for any evidence of the change of name or evidence the child uses the new name for all official purposes.
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Deal with the application, in line with current guidance and issue the passport in the new name on the court order.
Court orders that refer to the child in a different name
We will not accept a court order as evidence a child has changed their name when it simply refers to the child in a different name. For example, it shows the child’s name under ‘Name’, ‘Full Name of Child’ or in the body of the court order.
When this happens, you must:
Ask the customer to provide:
evidence the child has changed their name and they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
the consent of everyone with parental responsibility (or a court order that allows a change of name without it)
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Court orders for children and young adults up to the age of 18
Some court orders extend to the child’s 18th birthday and include a statement that nobody can cause the child to be known by another name, without the court’s consent. These include:
child arrangement orders
special guardianship orders
care orders under section 31 of the Children’s Act
Even if the court order does not relate to a child’s change of name, the customer must send it to us so we can check it allows them to change the child’s name.
Court orders: changing a name when a child is in care
You must refer to Parental responsibility: children in care of the local authority, when dealing with applications for children in care of a local authority.
Where a child is in care in the UK, we will not accept an application that includes a change of name, unless we have either the:
consent of everyone with parental responsibility; or,
leave (permission) of the court
This is covered in:
Children Northern Ireland Order 1995
Children (Scotland) Act 1995
Court orders for children in care usually include a statement that, while it is in place, a child’s name cannot be changed without the consent of the court. If the court order does not include this, before we change the child’s name, we need:
evidence of the child’s change of name and that they use it for all official purposes; and,
either:
the consent of everyone with parental responsibility; or,
a court order that allows the change of name without the consent of everyone with parental responsibility
Some court orders grant parental responsibility, even though it may not be immediately clear on the order.
Changing a name when a child arrangement order is in place
When a child arrangement order is in place that confirms who the child must live with, the child’s surname cannot be changed (see section 13(1) of the Act), unless we have either the:
written consent of everyone with parental responsibility
court’s consent through a specific issue order
For any change of name, we still need:
the consent of everyone with parental responsibility
evidence of the change of name and that it is used for all official purposes
Changing a name when there’s a special guardianship order
When there’s a special guardianship order, we will need either:
the consent of everyone with parental responsibility before we can change any part of a child’s name
a court order that allows the change of name
Children under 16 who changed their own name
We will accept a change of name for children under 16, when they themselves have changed it, if:
everyone with parental responsibility has given their consent to the application in the child’s name
we have evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
This is because:
a child under 16 cannot complete a change of name until they are 16
those with parental responsibility, have accepted the child’s change of name, by sending us a signed passport application form
You must request additional consent to the change of name if you need it and confirm the consent is genuine when you receive it, before completing the child’s application.
Young adults with a change of name
For the purposes of this guidance, a young adult is someone aged 16 or 17 years old.
For the purposes of this guidance, a young adult is someone aged 16 or 17 years old.
Young adult customer changed their own name after they turned 16
If a 16 or 17 year old changes their own name after they turned 16, we will accept the name change, if all the following apply:
they give us evidence of the change of name
they give us evidence they use it for all official purposes
there are no court orders in place
If there is a court order in place for the 16 or 17 year old, you must check it to see what consent you need.
Where there is no court order, we will not:
need the consent of everyone with parental responsibility (as the 16 or 17 year old changed their own name after they turned 16)
accept any objections to the change of name from anyone with parental responsibility
This is because they submitted an adult passport application and consented to their own change of name after they turned 16. This means someone with parental responsibility cannot object to the change of name.
If the 16 or 17 year old changed their name because they changed gender, you must refer to customer change of name because they changed gender, to check what:
consent you need (as the rules are different when a child or 16 or 17 year old changes gender)
change of name evidence you need
Young adult customer changed their own name before they turned 16
If a 16 or 17 year old changed their own name before they turned 16, see Children under 16 who changed their own name.
If the 16 or 17 year old cannot provide consent, they can provide a new change of name document they have completed themselves. See Customer changed their own name after they turned 16.
If there is a court order in place for the 16 or 17 year old, you must check it to see what consent you need.
If the 16 or 17 year old changed their name because they changed gender, you must refer to customer change of name because they changed gender, to check what:
consent you need (as the rules are different when a child or 16 or 17 year old changes gender)
change of name evidence you need
When someone else changed their name before they turned 16
If a 16 or 17 year old applies for a passport with a change of name and it was a third party (for example, a parent) who changed it before they turned 16, we will accept it, as long as:
they give us evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
there are no court orders in place
we have consent from all who have parental responsibility
If the 16 or 17 year old cannot provide consent, they can provide a new change of name document they have completed themselves. See Customer changed their own name after they turned 16.
If there is a court order in place for the 16 or 17 year old, you must check it to see what consent you need.
If the 16 or 17 year old changed their name because they changed gender, you must refer to customer change of name because they changed gender, to check what:
consent you need (as the rules are different when a child or 16 or 17 year old changes gender)
change of name evidence you need
When someone else changed their name after they turned 16
If a 16 or 17 year old applies for a passport with a change of name and it was a third party (for example, a parent) who changed it after they turned 16, we will accept, it if:
they give us evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
there are no court orders in place
If the 16 or 17 year old has applied for a passport in their new name, we can accept they have consented to the change of name and we do not need the consent of everyone with parental responsibility.
If there is a court order in place for the 16 or 17 year old, you must check it to see what consent you need.
If the 16 or 17 year old changed their name because they changed gender, you must refer to customer change of name because they changed gender, to check what:
consent you need (as the rules are different when a child or 16 or 17 year old changes gender)
change of name evidence you need
Third party application
We will not accept an application from a third party for a 16 or 17 year old whose name changed, unless it is because the 16 or 17 year old:
needs a third party to complete the application (see Confirming consent from third parties)
has a court order in place
Court orders or if the customer cannot give consent
If there is a court order or the 16 or 17 year old cannot give consent, we need:
evidence of the 16 or 17 year old’s change of name and evidence they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
evidence that shows the 16 or 17 year old cannot give consent
the court order (which means the 16 or 17 year old cannot consent or needs additional consent)
the consent of everyone with parental responsibility (see Confirming identity: checking a signature is genuine)
If the third party gives evidence to show the 16 or 17 year old cannot give consent, you must:
check it to see if it confirms the 16 or 17 year old cannot give consent
discuss the case with your operational team leader (if you have doubts)
add a case note to record your actions and the decisions you made, including what evidence you received
If we do not get the evidence to show the customer cannot give consent, you must raise a guidance query with Quality Examination Support team (QuESt). QuESt will confirm whether you can accept the change of name.
If there’s no court order or a reason why the 16 or 17 year old cannot give consent, you must refuse the application. The 16 or 17 year old must apply for their own passport.
False name changes: passport issued in error
We may find that the person who sent the application has made a false declaration to change a child’s name.
You must:
Refer the application for investigation along with confirmation of any written disputes. Public Protection report such cases to the police, who will decide whether to take legal action.
Send a letter to the person who made the application to explain the situation and tell them that unless there is a court order that consents to the name change:
they must return the passport within 2 weeks so we can cancel it
we will issue a new passport in their old name, valid up to the expiry date on the old passport
Send a new application form (but you may be able to reopen to reissue). You will need new photos if you cannot reopen to reissue or if a referee needs to confirm them.
Not ask for evidence for the use of the name for all official purposes.
If the person who made the application does not respond after 2 weeks, you must:
Send them a first reminder and allow 2 weeks for the customer to respond.
Send a second and final reminder, if they do not respond 2 weeks after we sent the first reminder. The reminder must tell the customer you will cancel the passport, if they do not respond. Send the reminder by Royal Mail ‘Signed For delivery’, unless:
the address is in an area where secure delivery signatures are mandatory, in which case, send it by secure delivery
it is an international address, in which case, send it by DHL
Add a passport note to show all the actions and decisions made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
If the person who made the application still does not respond, you must raise a guidance query.
QuESt will respond, taking into account:
if you must cancel the passport
what case notes you must add
if you must add a watchlist entry to stop any more passports being issued for the child to the person who made the false declaration
Passport issued in error with child’s name changed
There may be times when we find we issued a passport in error. For example, we issued it in the child’s new name without the consent of everybody with parental responsibility.
When dealing with such cases, you, the examiner, must:
Send a letter to the person who made the application, to explain the situation and tell them unless there is a court order that consents to the child’s change of name:
to return the passport within 2 weeks so you cancel it
you will issue a new passport in the child’s old name, valid up to the expiry date on the old passport
Send them a new application form. If we were at fault, send a pre-paid envelope and tell them we will refund the cost of the photos.
Not ask for evidence for the use of the name for all official purposes.
If the person who made the application does not respond after 2 weeks, you must:
Send them a first reminder and allow 2 weeks for them to respond.
Send a second and final reminder, if they do not respond 2 weeks after we sent the first reminder. The reminder must tell the customer you will cancel the passport, if they do not respond. Send the reminder by Royal Mail Signed For delivery, unless:
the address is in an area where secure delivery signatures are mandatory, in which case, send it by secure delivery
it is an international address, in which case send it by DHL
Add a passport note to show all actions taken and decisions made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
If the person who made the application still does not respond, you the examiner must:
Tell the person who raised the complaint (if there is one), that:
we have done what we can to investigate their complaint
they can raise the issue with the police, if they wish to take it further with the person who made the application
Not disclose any personal or sensitive information about the child or the person who made the application to the person who raised the complaint.
Arrange for the child’s name to be added to the watchlist so we can resolve the issue when they return the passport (for example, as part of a renewal application).
Add a passport note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Arrange for the child’s name to be added to the watchlist so we can resolve the issue when they return the passport (for example, as part of a renewal application).
When we get another application for the child, you must:
cancel the old passport on our passport records
resolve any issues with the child’s name, before you issue a new passport
DAP: change of name task
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff how to deal with the Change of name task on Digital Application Processing (DAP).
If the customer has changed their name from that recorded in an old passport (that is in our records), Digital Application Processing (DAP) will create a Change of name task. This task is one of the Change of personal details tasks.
You must:
Check the customer’s personal details (for example, their previous name and new name).
View the document (in the Document tab), and the results of the validation checks.
Record your decision for the task:
accept the change of name
ask the customer for another document
Complete additional checks if you have fraud concerns and decide if you need to refer the application for investigation.
How to check the document
You must:
Click on View document to open the document.
Check that the old and new names on the document match the old and new names on the DAP application, using the Names – evidence to change a name guidance.
Close the View document screen.
How to accept a customer’s new name
If the old and new names on the document match the old and new names on DAP and you have no other concerns with the application, you must:
Select Yes in Do you accept the change of name?
Add a case note to record your decision and any other information (for example, the date of marriage ceremony).
Click Save to record your decision.
If you have fraud concerns with a change of name
If you have fraud concerns about a change of name, you must:
Complete additional checks, as required by following the guidance.
Select No in Do you accept the change of name?
Add a case note to explain why you are referring the application for investigation.
Click Save to record your decision.
DAP will automatically refer the application for investigation.
If you need to ask for a document
If you need the customer to send a document as evidence of their change of name you must:
Send an email to the customer asking for a new document.
Select Not sure, ask for new documents, in Do you accept the change of name?
Add a case note to explain why you are asking for new documents. For example, the case note could say ‘document is laminated’.
Click Save.
Name changes before or during naturalisation or registration
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff how to deal with changes of name, before the customer has naturalised or registered.
You must refer to Name changes after a customer has naturalised or registered, if the customer changed their name after naturalisation or registration.
If a customer has changed their name before or during the naturalisation or registration process, the name on their passport application may not match the name on their certificate.
The customer must tell UK Visas and Immigration (UKVI) if they changed their name before or during the naturalisation or registration process. This is because the new name must be on the nationality certificate.
To deal with a passport application where the customer has changed their name before or during naturalisation or registration, you must:
Use UKVI systems to check if UKVI were aware the customer changed their name before or during naturalisation or registration.
Make sure you record the previous name in a case note.
Consider if the customer does or does not need to attend an interview.
Case note your actions, decisions and outcomes.
Name changes after naturalisation or registration
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff how to deal with changes of name or differences with the name, after the customer has naturalised or registered and how name related risks that mean the customer may need to attend an interview.
You must refer to Name changes before or during naturalisation or registration, if the customer changed their name before or during naturalisation or registration.
If a customer has changed their name after they naturalised or registered, the name on their passport application will not match the name on the naturalisation certificate.
Where the customer’s name on the passport application is different to the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate, you must make sure the customer is the rightful owner of the document.
Make sure you record the previous name in a case note
Check why the customer has changed their name (See Change of surname: marriage or civil partnership).
Check you have the necessary evidence needed for change of name and name in use (where required).
Check if the customer does not or does need to attend an interview.
Refer the application details to Public Protection.
Case note your actions, decisions and outcomes.
No interview: name changed after naturalisation or registration
If the customer changed their name because they married or changed gender (after they naturalised or registered) they do not need an interview, as long as:
they made their passport application within 1 year of naturalisation
there are no other fraud risks
Change of surname: marriage or civil partnership
If the customer’s surname has changed because they got married or entered into a civil partnership, you must be satisfied with how the name has been changed by looking at the names on the:
marriage or civil partnership certificate
naturalisation or registration certificate
You must be able to see how the name has been made up and you can see the link between the previous and new name.
You must:
Accept the change of name.
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
The customer’s surname may have changed because they are married or have a civil partnership and the change happened before they were issued with their naturalisation or registration certificate.
You must:
Tell the customer to send us:
a signed statement that they are using their married name for all official purposes
their marriage certificate or civil partnership certificate (if we do not already have it) and evidence they use their married name for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
Put the application on hold, while you wait for them to respond.
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Issue the passport in the name shown on the marriage or civil partnership certificate.
Name change not through marriage or a civil partnership
If the customer’s name has changed and it is not because they have married or entered into a civil partnership and there is no evidence the customer has changed their name, you must:
Contact the customer by phone to tell them we will issue their passport in the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Update the name on the system so it matches the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Add a case note to show all of the actions and decision you made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Issue the passport using the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
If the customer does not want us to use the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate, you must:
Ask them to provide evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Add a case note to show all actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Name on the application form in a different order to documents
The names on the application form may be in a different order (including the surname) to the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate and the customer has not provided evidence to show they have changed their name.
You must:
Tell the customer we will issue their passport in the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Update the name on the system so it matches the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Issue the passport using the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
The customer may tell us they do not want us to use the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate. If they do you must:
Ask them to provide evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Forenames on the application form are different to the documents
The forenames on the application form may be in a different order to those on the naturalisation or registration certificate and the customer has not provided evidence they have changed their name.
You must:
Tell the customer we will issue their passport in the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Update the name on the system so it matches the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Issue the passport using the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
The customer may not want the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate to show in the passport.
You must:
Ask them to provide evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Documents show additional forenames
The naturalisation or registration certificate may have additional forenames to the name on the passport application form, but the order of the names has not changed.
You must:
Tell the customer we will issue their passport in the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Update the name on the system so it matches the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
Add a case note to explain why you added the observation (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Issue the passport using the name shown on the naturalisation or registration certificate.
The customer may not want the name on the naturalisation or registration certificate to show in the passport.
You must:
Ask them to provide evidence of the change of name and that they use it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name).
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you have made (see Names: name related case notes for what you must include in the case note).
Foreign passport: name does not match
You must not tell the customer to return their naturalisation or registration certificate to UKVI when they issued it in a correct name but it does not match the name on their foreign passport. Instead, you must deal with the application, in line with the Names: aligning names on foreign documents guidance.
Name changes when the customer was issued with a status letter
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff how to deal with passport applications when the customer changed their name after they were issued with a status letter.
If the customer has changed their name from the name shown on the Home Office status letter, you must
follow Windrush: change of name after status letter guidance
refer to Name changes after a customer has naturalised or registered, treating the status letter as if it were a naturalisation or registration certificate
Customer change of name because they have changed gender
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff how to deal with passport applications when the customer (adult or child), has changed their name as they have changed gender. When dealing with change of gender applications, you must also refer to the gender recognition guidance.
When using this guidance to change a customer’s name, you the examiner must refer to Names: name related case notes to make sure the case notes include all correct information.
In line with the gender recognition guidance, you must not use the case notes to record any:
unnecessary references to a customer’s gender reassignment
references to surgery or treatment
any personal opinions or assumptions
System checks: customer has changed gender
You must carry out checks on passport records to make sure there is not an existing or expired passport held in a previous version of the name.
Evidence to change a name due to a change of gender
Where a customer has changed their name due to a change of gender, the evidence we need to support their passport application will depend on if the customer has a full or interim Gender Recognition Certificate (GRC).
No full or interim Gender Recognition Certificate
Customers may change their name because they have changed gender but do not have a full or interim Gender Recognition Certificate, for example, because they:
are under the age of 18 and cannot get one
have not applied for their change of gender to be legally recognised with the Gender Recognition Panel
If the customer does not have a GRC, they must provide us with a letter that requests a change of gender, and:
evidence the gender change is likely to be permanent (for example, a signed letter from a medical professional, for example, consultant or GP on headed paper)
evidence that their name has changed and that they use it for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
the written consent of everyone with parental responsibility to change the:
gender, if the person changing gender is under the age of 18 (in line with the authorisation and consent guidance and the gender recognition guidance)
the name, if the person changing gender is also changing their name and is under the age of 16
If the customer cannot give us evidence they use the new name for all purposes:
You must raise a guidance query and include scans of all supporting documents to the Quality and Examination Support team (QuESt).
Add a case note to show all the actions and decisions you made.
Put the application on hold, while you wait for them to respond.
If the customer has a full or interim GRC
If the customer has a full or interim GRC, we will accept it as evidence of the change of name. You must not ask for:
any other evidence of the change of name
evidence the name is in use, unless there is information to suggest they may not be using the name for all purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
Customer reverted to their old gender: changed name
If the customer has changed their name because they have reverted to their old gender, we need evidence:
of the change of name
that they use the name for all official purposes, including if it is their previous name or a new name (see Names: evidence to change a name)
that the gender they are reverting to is likely to be permanent (for example, a letter from a medical professional, for example a consultant or GP)
Customer adopts the dress and manner of the opposite sex
If a customer has changed their name because they have adopted the dress and manner of the opposite sex, they must provide evidence of:
their preferred identity, in line with the Gender Recognition guidance
the change of name and that they use it for all official purposes (see Names: evidence to change a name)
We will not issue a passport in the customer’s new name, if it’s being used for some but not all official purposes.
Foreign passport: name changed due to change of gender
When a customer changes their name because they have changed gender and hold a foreign passport, they must change the name on it to meet our Names: aligning names on foreign documents guidance.
Name changes: BOC, BOTC and BN(O) applications
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff about the extra requirements when British overseas citizens (BOCS) and British overseas territory citizens (BOTCs) have a change of name. It also tells them how to deal with minor changes we accept for British national (overseas) (BN(O)) applications.
You must also refer to changing an adults name or child’s name, which provides detailed guidance on dealing with applications that have a change of name.
You must deal with:
BOC applications, in line with the British overseas citizen’s guidance (BOC)
BOTC applications, in line with the British overseas territory citizen’s guidance (BOTC)
BN(O) applications, in line with the British national (overseas) guidance (BNO)
Only examiners who have had full nationality or complex nationality training, will deal with BOC, BOTC and BN(O) applications when there is a full change of name.
When a BOC, BOTC, or BN(O) has a change of name
All BOC, BOTC, BN(O) and British citizen passports must be in the same name (see Multiple British passports and nationality statuses)
Before we issue a British citizen or variant passport, you must tell the customer to give us evidence that shows they have changed the name in their other passport and dual national passports, first.
Confirming identity and nationality: BOC change of name
You must reconfirm the nationality and identity of BOCs, when:
they have a change of name or change in spelling, from the name on their source documents
a previous BOC passport has the observation ‘the holder is also known as [name]’, and it was not added to show we applied an exception to when the customer must align their name (see Names: aligning names on foreign documents)
You must not automatically keep the observation ‘the holder is also known as [name]’ on the new passport. You must only keep the observation after careful consideration and in line with this guidance.
BN(O) customer has double barrelled name following marriage
Some customer’s previous BN(O) passport may be in doubled barrelled surname following marriage (made of up their maiden and husbands name), even though they may have:
took their married name and only use that name
kept their maiden name and only use that name
This is because at the time the customer made their application for their previous BN(O) passport, they may have been told they had to apply using the double barrelled name. Their Permanent Identity Care (PIC) and HKSAR (Hong Kong Special Administrative Region) passport will be in the correct name (for example, their married or maiden name).
Customer states they only use their married or maiden name
If the customer tells you, they do not use the double barrelled name and only use their married (or maiden) you must:
ask them for:
their marriage certificate (to show how the double barrelled name was made up)
evidence they use the name for all official purposes (you may accept the PIC, HKSAR and address evidence)
accept the name on the application when all of the following apply:
you can see how the name was made up from the marriage certificate
the name on the application matches the name on the PIC, HKSAR (and any other foreign passport they hold) and address evidence
If the customer cannot provide their marriage certificate (or does not want to), you must ask them for evidence:
of a change of name (to show a change of name from the double barrelled name to the name they use)
evidence they use the name for all official purposes (you may accept the PIC, HKSAR and address evidence)
Names and change of names for diplomats and officials
This section tells His Majesty’s Passport Office operational staff about the extra requirements for Diplomats and officials who have a change of name. You must also refer to changing an adults name or child’s name, which provides detailed guidance on dealing with applications that have a change of name.
Passports for diplomats, British officials or King’s Messenger Services must be in the same name as their standard British passport. (see Multiple British passports and nationality statuses). If they do not have one, they must apply for one using the same name and wait for it to be issued.
If there is a change of name, we will not issue a passport in the new name until all valid passports have been sent to us to change.

https://www.gov.uk/government/publicatio.title: UKSV National Security Vetting: change of personal circumstances
https://www.gov.uk/government/publicatio.textContent:
If you hold a DV, SC, Level 1B or CTC security clearance and there is a significant change to your personal circumstances you should notify UKSV.
UKSV requires Change of Personal Circumstances (CPC) forms to be submitted via the NSVS portal.
The below link allows access to the CPC service via NSVS for valid clearance holders. Once you receive the CPC activation email and open the link, you may find you are logged into another account which you have accessed recently (such as a Security Appraisal Form). Please ensure that you log out first, before clicking on the link in the activation email for a second time. You can log out out via the option at the top right of your portal homepage.
Click this link to access the CPC portal service via NSVS.
In exceptional circumstances, please contact our UKSV Helpdesk for support completing the Change of Personal Circumstances (CPC) form manually.
How to contact UKSV
Once we authorise this request for the CPC form, you will then receive an email from UKSV which provides the form for completion, along with a secure link to a file-sharing service called Egress. This is used to ensure that any information shared either by you or with you is done so in a secure and safe manner. Instructions on how to upload and download information to and from Egress will be provided along with the link.
When to inform UKSV of a change of personal circumstances
As a holder of national security clearance, you have a responsibility to report any change in your personal circumstances which could potentially affect your clearance, using the process set out above. You are required to report the following events:
Change of name (please note we do not automatically require a CPC if you get married to a current partner but if you change your name for any reason, including marriage, we will require a CPC - please see the guidance below)
Change of nationality
New partner. The definition of a partner, for security vetting purposes, is either your spouse, a cohabiting partner, someone with whom you are in an enduring sexual and/or romantic relationship, or someone with whom you see a committed or enduring future
Divorce, or dissolution of a Civil Partnership
Involvement with the Police (if you are arrested, refused bail, have received a police caution, reprimand or warning, or are convicted of an offence - other than minor road traffic offences)
SC/DV holders only; Significant change in financial circumstances (bankruptcy, receiving a large inheritance, suffering substantial financial impact due to divorce or the dissolution of a civil partnership)
DV holders only; Change of co-resident (lodger, housemate, au pair, live-in domestic staff).
If you have changed your gender, there is currently no need to update UKSV with this information, and we do not require a copy of your Gender Recognition Certificate (GRC) as gender change is not a national security concern.
However, if you have changed your name for any reason, including marriage or gender change, then we will need to be informed of this.
UKSV requires a Change of Personal Circumstance form when someone has received a legal document confirming a change of name, such as:
marriage or civil partnership certificate
overseas marriage or civil partnership certificate
enrolled deed poll
unenrolled deed poll or change of name deed
statutory declaration or affidavit
baptismal or confirmation certificate (for first names only)
birth certificate
certificate of naturalisation or registration
adoption order/certificate
Application Form 24 (recording Changes of Forename(s) and Surname(s) in Scotland)
Whilst there is no requirement to update UKSV regarding a change in gender, if you;
Have changed your gender but you haven’t changed your name legally
Have changed your pronouns
Have not yet received your legal documents
Intend on keeping your name as it is legally but would like to add an alias
You are very welcome to use the NSVS portal to update us of this, using the change of name section and adding more detail. To reiterate, in these circumstances this is a personal choice, and your security clearance will not be impacted if you do not do this.
We would encourage all applicants that in any future interactions with us, such as a clearance renewal interview, you inform us of how you would like to be addressed, including name and pronouns, to ensure that any conversations with you are respectful and inclusive.
More information on your data and privacy can be found on this link.
